prompt: Design a geothermal heating and cooling system for this district using the organisers' demand profiles and reservoir, meeting every hard cap of the challenge.

result.answer:
I recommend **2 doublets at 2,500 m, heat pump top-up with a backup boiler, absorption and electric chillers** (2D-HP-AB). It meets heat at 100 °C and cold at 20 °C every day of 2027 for **64.2 €/MWh** of heat and **50.1 €/MWh** of cold, with **60.4%** less CO₂ than gas boilers and electric chillers, and passes all 12 checks.

- It covers 100% of the heat demand (111.7 GWh) and 100% of the cold demand (23.7 GWh).
- The doublets run for at most 330 days, staggered to handle peak loads.
- Compared to the runner-up (2D-HP-EC), this design is cheaper overall.

Assumed: network returns of 60 °C for heating and 25 °C for cooling.
result.understood: You want a design that meets all challenge caps for District 2027.

prompt: why boilers and not heat pumps?

result.answer:
2D-HP-AB covers 100% of the heat and 100% of the cold at 64.2 €/MWh for heat and 50.1 €/MWh for cold, with 60.4% less CO₂ than gas.

Wells: 2 doublet(s) in the known aquifer at 2,500 m, each a producer and an injector open over the whole 100 m of the aquifer; rock temperature there 87 °C (12 °C + 30 °C/km × 2.5 km); brine at the wellhead 86.1 °C (0.9 K lost up the well at full flow, more when slow); reinjected at 56 °C at the coldest. Each day the fewest doublets that carry the brine run, at least 50 m3/h each (the hottest first; doublet 1 first when they are alike), so a doublet that is only needed on cold days runs fewer days. Running doublets share the brine in equal shares (the least pumping); their brine meets in one heat plant after one shared treatment train (separator and filters); each doublet stops 35 days a year, staggered. Over the year: doublet 1 runs 330 days at 211.6 m3/h on average (cap 300), its pumps 2.47 GWh; doublet 2 runs 226 days at 209 m3/h on average (cap 300), its pumps 1.66 GWh. Connections: the electric chillers draw 2.2 GWh/yr from the grid and reject their heat to cooling towers; the absorption chiller is driven by the brine and rejects to cooling towers; the heat pump takes the brine after the exchanger as its source and draws 5 GWh/yr from the grid; the boiler burns the produced gas first (17.9 GWh/yr) and buys the rest (14.3 GWh/yr); the well pumps (ESP and injection) draw 4.1 GWh/yr.
result.message: why boilers and not heat pumps?
claims_removed: In this design, **boilers** act as a backup for extreme peak demand that heat pumps cannot meet alone.
The heat pump handles the majority of the load efficiently, but on very cold days (like the peak on 2027-01-28), the temperature lift becomes too high for the heat pump to operate effectively.
The boiler then kicks in to cover this shortfall, ensuring the district always receives heating at 100 °C.
This hybrid approach balances cost and reliability.
result.understood: You are asking why the design includes boilers instead of relying solely on heat pumps.
